title: Sweet potato tissue in sucrose solutions
stem: Cylinders of sweet potato tissue were blotted, weighed and placed in sucrose solutions for 18 hours at 20 °C, then blotted and reweighed. Six cylinders were used per concentration (n = 6).

data.caption: Mean mass of sweet potato cylinders before and after 18 hours in sucrose solution

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean percentage change in mass for the cylinders in 0.6 mol dm⁻³ sucrose.
markscheme: −7.5 % / −7.53 % (negative sign or 'decrease' required)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Estimate the sucrose concentration at which there would be no net change in mass of the tissue.
markscheme: zero change lies between 0.2 and 0.4 mol dm⁻³ / closer to 0.4
0.38 mol dm⁻³ (Allow 0.35–0.40)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the change in mass of the cylinders in 0.8 mol dm⁻³ sucrose in terms of water potential.
markscheme: solution has a lower/more negative solute potential than the cell sap
water potential of the solution is lower than that of the cells
water moves by osmosis from higher to lower water potential / out of cells
through partially permeable membranes / aquaporins
pressure potential of cells falls / cells become flaccid / plasmolysis
loss of water reduces mass by 13.7 %

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest why percentage change in mass is used rather than change in mass.
markscheme: cylinders had different initial masses / allows fair comparison between cylinders of different mass

title: A dihybrid cross in an ornamental plant
stem: In an ornamental plant, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white flowers (p) and hairy leaves (H) are dominant to smooth leaves (h). Two plants heterozygous for both genes (PpHh) were crossed and 320 offspring were scored. Critical values of χ² at p = 0.05: 1 df = 3.84; 2 df = 5.99; 3 df = 7.81.

data.caption: Phenotypes of offspring from the cross PpHh × PpHh

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the expected number of white, smooth offspring if the genes assort independently.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the chi-squared value for these results, assuming an expected ratio of 9:3:3:1.
markscheme: expected values 180, 60, 60, 20

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Deduce, with reference to the critical value, whether the results support a 9:3:3:1 ratio.
markscheme: 3 degrees of freedom / critical value 7.81
0.89 < 7.81 so difference not significant / accept null hypothesis
results consistent with 9:3:3:1 / independent assortment / differences due to chance

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how a 9:3:3:1 ratio arises from this cross.
markscheme: genes are unlinked / on different chromosomes
independent assortment during meiosis I / random orientation of bivalents
each parent produces four gamete types PH, Ph, pH, ph in equal proportions
random fertilisation gives 16 equally likely combinations
9 have at least one P and one H / 1 is pphh (double recessive)
Allow: Punnett grid correctly drawn

title: Earlier flowering of a woodland cherry
stem: The date of first flowering of 40 marked wild cherry trees in one woodland was recorded every ten years, together with the mean air temperature for March and April.

data.caption: Mean spring temperature and mean date of first flowering (n = 40 trees)
columns: Mean first-flowering date / day of year

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mean rate of change in first-flowering date between 1990 and 2020, in days per decade.
markscheme: −5 days per decade / 5 days earlier per decade

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the relationship between spring temperature and first-flowering date.
markscheme: negative correlation / higher temperature, earlier flowering
temperature rose by 1.8 °C while flowering advanced by 15 days
about 8 days earlier per 1 °C rise
relationship appears consistent across all four years

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the hypothesis that rising spring temperatures cause the cherry trees to flower earlier.
markscheme: supports: flowering earlier in every decade as temperature rises
supports: SD ranges for 1990 (122–134) and 2020 (107–119) do not overlap, so the change is likely significant
limitation: correlation does not prove causation
limitation: only four data points / one woodland / one species
limitation: other factors may have changed (e.g. day length unchanged, tree age, rainfall, CO₂)
limitation: same trees are getting older over 30 years
an experiment controlling temperature would be needed
parts.notes: At least one supporting and one limiting point for full marks.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest how earlier flowering could affect insect populations that pollinate the trees.
markscheme: flowering may no longer coincide with insect emergence / phenological mismatch
insects emerging later find less nectar/pollen, reducing survival/reproduction
fewer flowers pollinated, reducing fruit/seed set
Allow: insect emergence may also shift if triggered by temperature, maintaining synchrony

title: Glucose tolerance in two groups of adults
stem: Adults without diabetes (group A, n = 15) and adults with type 2 diabetes (group B, n = 15) fasted overnight and then drank a solution containing 75 g glucose at time 0. Blood glucose concentration was measured every 30 minutes.

data.caption: Mean blood glucose concentration after a glucose drink

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage increase in mean blood glucose concentration of group A between 0 and 30 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare and contrast the changes in blood glucose concentration in groups A and B.
markscheme: both increase after the glucose drink
group B higher at all times / starts higher (7.4 vs 5.0 mmol dm⁻³)
group A peaks at 30 min whereas group B peaks later at 60 min
group B peak higher (14.1 vs 8.1 mmol dm⁻³)
group A returns almost to fasting level by 120 min whereas group B remains high (11.2 mmol dm⁻³)
group B more variable / larger SD

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how blood glucose concentration in group A returns to near its fasting level.
markscheme: rise in glucose detected by β cells in pancreatic islets
β cells secrete insulin
insulin causes body cells/muscle to take up glucose (more glucose transporters)
liver and muscle cells convert glucose to glycogen / glycogenesis
glucose used in respiration / converted to fat
negative feedback: insulin secretion falls as glucose falls

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suggest one reason why glucose stays high in group B.
markscheme: body cells less responsive to insulin / insulin resistance / fewer or faulty insulin receptors
Allow: reduced insulin secretion by β cells
parts.notes: Reject 'no insulin produced' as this describes type 1.

title: From DNA to polypeptide
stem: Before a cell divides its DNA is copied, and throughout its life genes are expressed as polypeptides.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the name of the enzyme that separates the two strands of DNA during replication.
markscheme: helicase

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Outline why DNA replication is described as semi-conservative.
markscheme: each strand of the original molecule acts as a template
new strand assembled by complementary base pairing
each new DNA molecule contains one original/parent strand and one new strand

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how the base sequence of an mRNA molecule determines the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide.
markscheme: mRNA read in triplets of bases / codons
each codon specifies one amino acid / genetic code
tRNA anticodon pairs with the complementary codon
each tRNA carries a specific amino acid
ribosome moves along mRNA in 5′ to 3′ direction one codon at a time
peptide bonds join amino acids in the order set by codons
start codon (AUG) sets reading frame; stop codon ends translation

title: Cell division in garlic root tips
stem: A student prepared a squash of a garlic root tip and classified 500 cells by the stage of the cell cycle.

data.caption: Number of cells in each stage of the cell cycle

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mitotic index for this root tip.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Outline the events that occur during prophase of mitosis.
markscheme: chromosomes condense/supercoil / become visible
each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at centromere
nuclear membrane breaks down
spindle microtubules begin to form

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Distinguish between the outcomes of mitosis and meiosis.
markscheme: mitosis: two daughter nuclei whereas meiosis: four
mitosis: diploid/same chromosome number whereas meiosis: haploid/halved
mitosis: genetically identical whereas meiosis: genetically different

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how meiosis generates genetic variation.
markscheme: crossing over between non-sister chromatids in prophase I
exchange of alleles produces new combinations on a chromatid
random orientation of bivalents/homologous pairs in metaphase I
independent assortment of unlinked genes
2ⁿ possible combinations (2²³ in humans)
random orientation of chromatids in metaphase II (after crossing over)

title: Epigenetic control of gene expression
stem: Identical (monozygotic) twins have the same DNA base sequence, but differences in their patterns of gene expression can increase as they age.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the effect of histone acetylation on transcription.
markscheme: increases transcription / chromatin less condensed so genes more accessible to RNA polymerase

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how methylation of DNA in a promoter region can silence a gene.
markscheme: methyl groups added to cytosine (in CpG sites)
transcription factors/RNA polymerase cannot bind the promoter
methylated DNA attracts proteins that condense chromatin / histone deacetylation
tightly packed chromatin/heterochromatin is not transcribed
no mRNA produced so no polypeptide
methylation pattern can be passed on in cell division

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suggest reasons why the methylation patterns of monozygotic twins become more different with age.
markscheme: different environments/diet/smoking/stress alter methylation
random errors in copying methylation patterns accumulate with each division
longer time for differences to accumulate
different illnesses/exposure to toxins / OWTTE

title: Hormones and human reproduction
stem: Human reproduction depends on gametes produced by meiosis and on hormonal coordination.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare and contrast sexual and asexual reproduction.
markscheme: both produce new individuals / increase population
sexual involves two parents whereas asexual one parent
sexual involves meiosis and fertilisation of gametes whereas asexual uses mitosis only
sexual offspring genetically different whereas asexual offspring are clones
sexual generates variation useful in a changing environment
asexual faster / no need to find a mate / can rapidly colonise a stable habitat
parts.notes: At least one similarity for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the roles of FSH and LH in the menstrual cycle.
markscheme: both secreted by the pituitary gland
FSH stimulates development of follicles
FSH stimulates follicle cells to secrete oestradiol
rising oestradiol causes a surge of LH (positive feedback)
LH surge triggers ovulation
LH stimulates development of the corpus luteum
corpus luteum secretes progesterone

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how hormones are used in in vitro fertilisation (IVF).
markscheme: drug/hormone (e.g. GnRH analogue) used to stop the normal cycle / down-regulation
stops pituitary secreting FSH and LH
allows timing of egg development to be controlled
large doses of FSH injected
causes many follicles to develop / superovulation
hCG injection (acts like LH) to mature the eggs
eggs collected before ovulation
eggs fertilised with sperm outside the body
progesterone given to maintain the endometrium
embryos transferred to the uterus after a few days
progesterone prevents breakdown of uterine lining / supports implantation

title: Selection and ecosystem stability
stem: Populations evolve through natural selection, while ecosystems may remain stable or undergo change.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline the requirements for evolution by natural selection to occur.
markscheme: variation between individuals in a population
variation must be heritable / caused by genes
sources of variation: mutation / meiosis / sexual reproduction
more offspring produced than the environment can support / overproduction
competition / struggle for survival
individuals better adapted survive and reproduce more
favourable alleles passed on, increasing in frequency over generations

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe features that allow an ecosystem to remain stable over long periods.
markscheme: supply of energy (sunlight) maintained
nutrients/matter recycled
high biodiversity / many species
complex food webs so loss of one species has less effect
genetic diversity within populations
climate within tolerance limits of organisms
limited human impact / no tipping point reached

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain, using a named example, how natural selection can change allele frequencies in a population.
markscheme: named example (e.g. antibiotic resistance in bacteria / beak size in Galápagos finches / insecticide resistance)
variation exists in the population for the trait
variation caused by different alleles (arising by mutation)
selection pressure named (e.g. antibiotic / drought changing seed size)
individuals with advantageous allele more likely to survive
they reproduce and pass on the allele
individuals without it die / produce fewer offspring
frequency of the advantageous allele increases over generations
if selection pressure continues population becomes adapted
named example correctly linked to selection pressure and outcome

title: Gene expression, mutation and gene editing
stem: Changes to the base sequence of a gene can alter the polypeptide it codes for, and these changes can now be made deliberately.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Outline the consequences of a base substitution mutation, using sickle cell anaemia as an example.
markscheme: one base replaced by another in the DNA sequence
in the haemoglobin beta gene, GAG becomes GTG
mRNA codon changes from GAG to GUG
glutamic acid replaced by valine (sixth amino acid)
haemoglobin forms fibres/crystallises at low oxygen
red blood cells become sickle-shaped / block capillaries / carry less oxygen
Allow: some substitutions are silent because the code is degenerate

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe how the CRISPR–Cas9 system can be used to knock out a gene.
markscheme: guide RNA designed complementary to target sequence in the gene
guide RNA combined with Cas9 nuclease
complex introduced into cell
guide RNA binds target DNA by complementary base pairing
Cas9 cuts both strands of DNA at the target site
cell's repair introduces errors/insertions/deletions
frameshift/stop codon so gene product non-functional / gene knocked out

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how a eukaryotic gene is transcribed and how the transcript is modified before translation.
markscheme: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter
transcription factors needed for binding
DNA unwound/strands separated by RNA polymerase
template/antisense strand used
free RNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases (uracil pairs with adenine)
RNA nucleotides linked in 5′ to 3′ direction
transcription ends at terminator; RNA released
5′ cap added
poly-A tail added at the 3′ end
introns removed by splicing / exons joined
alternative splicing gives different proteins from one gene
mature mRNA exits through nuclear pores
